claims.claim: In developmental terms, adult relationships are the close bonds of friendship, partnership, and care that shape adult life; they are the channel for relatedness, which self-determination theory identifies as a basic need alongside autonomy and competence (Ryan & Deci, via OpenStax Lifespan Development).

Friendships change over the course of early adulthood, and the changes are linked more closely to life transitions (starting college, beginning a career, changing romantic status, becoming a parent) than to age itself (Jeffrey Arnett's review, via OpenStax Lifespan Development 12.3).

Friendships deepen in early adulthood with increasing intimacy and trust; friendship networks expand in young adulthood as bonds form in daily settings (school, work, community), and the overall size of the social network steadily decreases from early to later adulthood (Wrzus et al., via OpenStax Lifespan Development 12.3 and 16.2).

Sternberg's triangular theory of love (1986) holds that love combines three components — passion (longing, excitement, attraction), intimacy (closeness and self-disclosure), and commitment (loyalty and reliability) — and their combinations produce different kinds of love, including companionate love (intimacy plus commitment, which also appears in friendships and family bonds) and consummate love (all three components).

The most fulfilling romantic relationships for young adults are characterized by intimacy, passion, and commitment (Bauermeister et al., via OpenStax Lifespan Development 12.5), and the three components vary across the lifespan: passion and intimacy peak in early adulthood and ease slightly in middle adulthood without disappearing (OpenStax 14.2).

Hazan and Shaver (1987) proposed that attachment security, first studied in infant-caregiver bonds, continues to matter across the lifespan and in adult romantic relationships; secure adult attachment is associated with better conflict resolution, mutual caring and trust, emotional closeness, and relationship satisfaction.

Adult relationships move through a life cycle of forming, maintaining, and ending: bonds form in shared settings and transitions, are kept alive by deliberate effort (shared time, disclosure, trust), and end when needs go unmet — most commonly in young adulthood when a partner does not meet the need for connection or does not support the need for independence (OpenStax 12.5); throughout life people gain new relationships and end old ones (social convoy, OpenStax 16.2).

Relationships take many forms: at any given time about half of young adults are single and singlehood is not developmentally problematic; companionate love exists across friendships, family, and other platonic relationships; and social networks are made of many different types of relationships.

Relationships are the scaffolding of adult development: high-quality supportive friendships in early adulthood predict psychological and physical health (OpenStax 12.3); people who stay connected with others and engage in meaningful activities feel a sense of purpose and tend to live longer (NIA); loneliness in later life is correlated with a range of health problems (OpenStax 16.2).

conflictingEvidence.issue: Do adult social networks grow or shrink over time?
positions: Friendship networks expand in young adulthood, and new friendships form in the new settings of adult life (Wrzus et al., via OpenStax 12.3).
The overall size of the social network steadily decreases from early to later adulthood (Wrzus et al., via OpenStax 16.2).
The social convoy view holds that people gain new relationships and end old ones throughout life (Kahn & Antonucci, via OpenStax 16.2).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both findings are presented with their time contexts: networks grow during young adulthood as transitions add new settings and friends, then gradually shrink from early to later adulthood; the lesson describes the whole arc rather than picking one direction.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is romantic love with all three Sternberg components the only 'full' love?
positions: Sternberg called love combining all three components (passion, intimacy, commitment) consummate or complete love (OpenStax 14.2).
Companionate love (intimacy plus commitment) is a real and common form that also exists across friendships and family bonds (OpenStax 14.2).
The components vary across the lifespan: passion and intimacy peak in early adulthood and ease slightly in middle adulthood while remaining present (OpenStax 14.2).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson treats love as combinations of components rather than a single ideal: consummate love is the fullest combination, but companionate love is described as a genuine, common form, and a bond shifting from consummate toward companionate is framed as normal change, not failure.

positions: Young adults most often end romantic relationships because a partner did not meet their need for connection or did not support their need for independence (OpenStax 12.5).
The social convoy view treats endings as a normal part of how relationships change over life: people gain new relationships and end old ones (OpenStax 16.2).
About half of young adults are single at any given time, and being single is not treated as developmentally problematic (OpenStax 12.5).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Endings are presented factually as part of the relationship life cycle, with the documented reasons (unmet needs) and without value judgments; singlehood after or between relationships is described as common and normal.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft made no factual claims; its placeholder boilerplate ('Relationships is a foundational concept in Human Development', 'a college-level explanation names the concept') was discarded wholesale and replaced with source-verified developmental content.
The draft's Eli-10 analogy ('a label on a toolbox drawer') was replaced; that phrasing is flagged as generic-draft residue by the acceptance gate.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the draft's abstract treatment of 'relationships' with the substantive developmental content: working definition (relatedness + social convoy), friendship change across life stages, Sternberg's triangular theory, the Hazan & Shaver attachment echo, and the forming-maintaining-ending life cycle.
Rebuilt all five practice questions as full 4-option items (the draft's quickCheck items had only 3 options) with keys verified against the evidence packet.

sourceRecords.notes: Tier A open textbook. Read via Wayback Machine capture (timestamp 20250518031258) because openstax.org blocks direct fetch.
